title: The AI-First Asset Manager
gist: BCG argues that autonomous AI agents, not copilots, can finally break asset management's structural link between costs and AUM: a manager running at 15-20bps could cut 3-6bps (25-30%), add 0.5-1% of AUM in annual net inflows from AI-enabled distribution within 3-5 years, and expand research coverage two to five times. The bigger claim is competitive, not operational: AI leaders in the industry already capture 3x the cost and revenue benefit of laggards, and BCG expects that gap to compound.

insights.claim: In asset management, costs have outpaced revenue for more than a decade despite heavy technology investment, because the shift to low-fee products compressed revenue while cost bases kept scaling.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Margin pressure in traditional asset managers is structural, not cyclical — do not underwrite mean-reversion in operating margins without an agentic-AI cost story.
insights.quote: Despite heavy tech investment, rising costs and the shift to low-fee products have led to costs outpacing revenue for more than a decade.
insights.locator: Asset managers are right to feel under pressure

insights.claim: Over the past 15 years global AUM has more than tripled and revenues more than doubled, yet asset-manager margins are essentially unchanged, because costs have historically scaled with assets.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Scale alone has never been an operating-leverage story in this industry — screen managers on cost-per-AUM trajectory, not AUM growth.
insights.quote: Over the past 15 years, global AUM has more than tripled, revenues have more than doubled, yet margins remain essentially unchanged, according to BCG’s Global Asset Management Report 2026.
insights.locator: AI Agents Break the Cost-AUM Link

insights.claim: A traditional asset manager operating at 15 to 20 basis points of cost that reshapes its organization to deploy AI at scale could cut expenses by 3 to 6 basis points, a 25% to 30% reduction.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Quantifies the upside: a 25-30% expense cut is a step-change in fee-pressure tolerance and a concrete re-rating trigger for listed managers that execute.
insights.quote: Early evidence suggests that a traditional asset manager with a cost of 15 to 20 basis points that reshapes their organization to deploy AI at scale could reduce expenses by 3 to 6 basis points, perhaps a 25% to 30% cut.
insights.locator: The new wave of AI—autonomous agents

insights.claim: Autonomous AI agents that execute complex multi-step workflows decouple costs from AUM, so that reinvesting the savings keeps the cost curve flat even as assets grow and AUM per head rises with limited marginal cost.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: AUM-per-head is the metric to track — it is the observable proxy for whether a manager has actually broken the cost-AUM link.
insights.quote: More fundamentally, AI agents decouple costs from AUM—and reinvesting the savings keeps that curve flat even as assets grow.
insights.locator: The rapid improvement in AI, particularly autonomous

insights.claim: AI-driven distribution efficiency lowers the minimum viable mandate size: a manager that previously served only custom mandates above $500 million can profitably offer them at significantly lower amounts, expanding the addressable client base.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: The mid-market institutional and wealth segment becomes contestable by large managers — a competitive threat to specialist boutiques serving smaller mandates.
insights.quote: A manager who previously handled only custom mandates above $500 million can now profitably offer them at significantly lower amounts.

insights.claim: BCG's modeling shows an AI-first asset manager can achieve incremental annual inflows of 0.5% to 1% of AUM within three to five years purely from deploying AI in distribution.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: A revenue, not just cost, argument — 50-100bps of extra organic flow per year is a material differentiator in an industry fighting for flat net flows.
insights.quote: But our modeling shows that an AI-first asset manager can, within three to five years, achieve incremental annual inflows of 0.5% to 1% of AUM just through deploying AI to support distribution.
insights.locator: Given this choice, impact can be highly variable

insights.claim: The typical investment workflow has been digitized but not reformed: analysts still manually monitor names on a terminal, read transcripts and filings, and present to investment committees that often lack time to prepare deeper questioning.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Identifies where the real inefficiency sits — decision quality at the IC, not data access — and points to where AI vendors can actually sell.
insights.quote: Today’s investment workflow has been digitized but remains generally unreformed.
insights.locator: AI Agents in Investment Research and Portfolio Construction

insights.claim: Analysts equipped with AI agents could monitor and conduct deep research on five times as many companies, with AI agents continuously scanning thousands of names and returning curated, ranked opportunities.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Coverage expansion favors strategies whose alpha comes from breadth — small/mid-cap and global mandates gain most relative to concentrated large-cap books.
insights.quote: In investment research, analysts equipped with AI agents could monitor and conduct deep research on five times as many companies.
insights.locator: But the more significant opportunity is broader

insights.claim: A committee of specialized AI agents can pre-brief an investment committee by systematically stress-testing the thesis — generating counterarguments, surfacing contradictory data, and flagging cognitive biases in the original analysis.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable process upgrade any allocator can adopt: adversarial agent review before capital is committed.
insights.quote: a committee of specialized AI agents can systematically stress-test the investment thesis—generating counterarguments, surfacing contradictory data, and flagging cognitive biases in the original analysis

insights.claim: AI can increase research coverage two to five times and support improvements in the Sharpe ratio, while shifting portfolio construction and risk analysis from weekly or monthly and siloed to real-time and responsive to changing correlations.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: If real, this is an alpha claim, not just an efficiency claim — watch for managers reporting Sharpe improvement attributable to AI-driven coverage.
insights.quote: AI can increase research coverage two to five times, supporting improvements in the Sharpe ratio.
insights.locator: Portfolio construction and risk analysis become real-time

insights.claim: Being an AI-first asset manager means reimagining how work gets done, not giving employees access to copilots — a distinction that separates genuine transformation from the widespread copilot rollouts already in the market.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: A cheap diligence filter: firms citing copilot seat counts as their AI strategy have not captured the economics described here.
insights.quote: This is the AI-first asset manager: not an organization that has given employees access to copilots, but one that has reimagined how work gets done.
insights.locator: This is the AI-first asset manager

insights.claim: Capturing the full AI opportunity requires the CEO, CTO, and CIO to align on a common strategic vision and then rebuild two or three high-value workflows end-to-end around agentic AI — for most managers, in research and distribution — with concrete P&L targets and budgets protected for at least three years.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Gives an observable checklist for judging whether a manager's AI program is credible: board mandate, multi-year protected budget, named workflows, P&L targets.
insights.quote: They should begin by selecting two or three high-value workflows and rebuilding them end-to-end around agentic AI.
insights.locator: Realizing the full opportunity, however, requires

insights.claim: Governance for agentic AI — auditability and human intervention points — must be designed in from day one because retrofitting it is much harder and often slows organizations down.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: A key execution risk: early movers without governance may stall at the scaling stage, handing the advantage to more deliberate competitors.
insights.quote: Retrofitting is much harder and often slows organizations down.

insights.claim: Only high-quality data lets AI agents deliver reliable results at scale, and most asset managers should adopt a hybrid tech strategy — buying is quicker, but in-house development delivers bespoke results and avoids vendor lock-in.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Supports demand for both enterprise data-infrastructure vendors and in-house agent-engineering talent, rather than a winner-take-all platform outcome.
insights.quote: buying systems is quicker, but in-house development delivers bespoke results and avoids lock-in
insights.locator: Establish the data and technology infrastructure

insights.claim: AI adoption in asset managers fails without incentive alignment — compensation and promotion must be tied to AI adoption and outcomes, because what is not in a scorecard or review usually does not happen.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Look for AI metrics in disclosed comp scorecards as the highest-signal evidence that a transformation is real.
insights.quote: If it is not in a scorecard or review, it usually will not happen.

insights.claim: In the near term agent-building engineers must be embedded inside asset-management business units, while long-term talent strategy has to evolve toward leaner, more agile organizations and widespread prompt-writing and agent-design skills from CEO to junior analyst.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Implies structural headcount decline in traditional middle/front-office roles alongside a bid for agent engineers — relevant to financial-services labor and comp trends.
insights.quote: In the near term, engineers skilled at building agents will need to be embedded in the business.
insights.locator: Plan to be the asset manager of the future

insights.claim: BCG's Build for the Future Survey 2025 finds AI leaders among asset managers are already capturing three times the average cost and revenue benefits of AI laggards.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Dispersion within the sector is already measurable — this argues for pair trades between AI-leading and AI-lagging listed asset managers rather than a sector call.
insights.quote: BCG’s Build for the Future Survey 2025 shows that AI leaders among asset managers are already achieving three times the average cost and revenue benefits as AI laggards.
insights.locator: BCG’s Build for the Future Survey 2025

insights.claim: The compounding nature of AI means the performance gap between AI leaders and laggards in asset management will widen, and the window to establish an AI-first strategy is open but will not stay open long.
insights.speaker: Joppe Bijlsma
insights.so_what: Frames a timing thesis: late adopters may face a permanent structural disadvantage, raising consolidation pressure on sub-scale managers.
insights.quote: The opportunity to develop an AI-first strategy is open, but it will not stay open long.
insights.locator: The inherently compounding nature of AI
